Human-AI collaboration through search-assisted task assistance, where end-users can initiate tasks using specific concepts and receive assistance in performing the task through natural language input, is a rapidly developing field. One critical component of this technology is search-assisted Concept Placement, where a user's selected concept is replaced by retrieving relevant information from non-textual sources such as images, videos, and URLs. Unlike conventional, multi-stage approaches, this paper introduces a novel, unified model to effectively integrate the identification of search phrases and concept placement. We propose SLIM, a system leveraging individualized, adaptive learning profiles and online exploration of the search space. Experiments on the search-assisted Concept Placement dataset, MIND dataset, and MS MARCO demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, with improvements of over 4 and 1.7 respectively.

In a pioneering approach, the impact of high-frequency sound waves on the characteristics of a colloidal gel was studied, marking the first instance where both the mechanical strength and flow behavior of the gel were adjusted through acoustic control. The gel's behavior was monitored using a technique called acoustic rheology, which revealed that applying stress through high-frequency sound waves initially weakens the gel, before strengthening it. The acoustic measurements, in turn, showed an acoustic modulus that fluctuated within a similar range as the mechanical gel's yield stress. When the sound amplitude was surpassed by a specific threshold, the mechanical properties of the gel softened and, further sound pressure resulted in a uniform gel-to-sol conversion of the entire sample. The findings indicate that the gel's microstructure, which comprises weak junctions that reorganize over time, responds to acoustic stress through the reorientation and, eventually, irreversible breakdown of the network under sufficient sound pressure.

The Collatz Conjecture poses a simple yet unresolved mathematical problem involving a specific map $T$, defined as follows for every positive integer $n$: 

  $$T(n) = \begin{cases}
 3n+1 & \text{if $n$ is odd}\\
n/2 & \text{if $n$ is even}
\end{cases}$$

Despite its apparent simplicity, the Conjecture has proven to be a notoriously difficult problem in modern mathematics. Defined as the assertion that every sequence generated by the conjecture eventually returns to the number one, the problem has so far only been verified for integers up to a value of $n \leq 2^{32}$ by means of direct computation. 

In this work, the underlying structure of the $T$ map is examined through a graph-theoretic lens, with the resulting analysis paving the way for a probabilistic approach to the Conjecture, thereby enabling it to be reframed as a fundamental event in a corresponding probabilistic space.

Understanding document content through computer vision is a crucial aspect of many tasks.
Currently, classifying STEM documents from a page image to its corresponding section remains an unresolved issue.
A widely used public dataset for document classification, namely the DOG, has been utilized.
Nevertheless, it is unclear whether the classifications are based on the document's mathematical or scientific nature.
To bridge this knowledge gap, we analyzed each document and classified it into specific categories using mathematical and scientific classes.
By leveraging knowledge graphs, we identified relationships between mathematical entities and visual clues present in the documents.
This study demonstrates that adding artificial mathematical and scientific information enhances the classification accuracy by 11.8%.
As a result, we have clarified how DOG is utilized and identified potential areas for improvement.
To further explore knowledge integration, we have created a novel dataset, namely the CSMD, which is designed for classifying STEM documents into mathematical and scientific categories.
The code and the dataset can be accessed at https://github.com/Seonghyeok-Lee/Document-Classification.

A buyer and seller exchange multiple signals indicating their true valuation,
with the highest bidder winning the item and paying its own signal as the price.
Given multiple opportunities to reveal signals, the buyer's problem is framed as
adversarially matching the seller's signals, yielding an algorithm that guarantees
a specific utility lower bound dependent solely on the history and not influenced
by future signals or the adversary's actions.
This result is further compared to the ideal scenario where both parties can
reveal signals just once, yielding a closed-form lower bound dependent on the
first few signals exchanged, and a conditional stronger bound is also provided.
The upper bound is shown to be equal to the ideal scenario where both parties
can reveal signals just once.
This finding is also true for a restricted setting in which the item values are
drawn from fixed distributions.
A final note discusses the impact of an item winner taking more than one item.

This paper presents SummScore, a novel evaluation metric that assesses the quality of summarizing by considering the importance of individual words within a document. Unlike traditional metrics, SummScore leverages the capabilities of the BERT model to compare a document and its summary, effectively capturing nuances in both monolingual and bilingual summarization. To demonstrate its efficiency, SummScore has been tested on four prominent multimodal and document summarization datasets, including the CNN/DailyMail and XSum datasets. The results indicate that SummScore surpasses current metrics like ROUGE,beit5, and BEERT in accurately measuring summarization quality. Notably, SummScore has a compact design, comprising 50 million learnable parameters, and a fast inference time of approximately 0.07 seconds per comparison, making it a practical and reliable evaluation metric for summarization tasks.

We develop and analyze the convergence properties of an algorithm that reconstructs a nonnegative, a priori unknown function from its quadratic measurements. The model is based on a compressed sensing framework and can be applied to various fields such as microscopy and quantum state tomography. Our analysis builds on recent work and extends it by proving that a signaling model can be exactly reconstructed if it follows a sparse or low-rank structure and is within a certain threshold of complexity. The model is non-convex due to the quadratic measurements and the signaling model's constraints, so we use an alternating minimization algorithm. The algorithm consists of two steps: a data fitting step and a denoising step. The data fitting step minimizes the difference between the estimated signal and the measurements, while the denoising step projects the estimate onto the nonnegative orthant or the sparse and low-rank sets. The complexity of this algorithm is high due to the denoising step's projection onto the low-rank Grassmannian manifold. However, if we replace the exact projection with a random initialization, the complexity of each iteration becomes the same as in the compressed sensing case. The complexity of the algorithm is high due to the data fitting step's numerical cost.

Fusion-based sensor integration is a promising approach to enhance sensor capabilities and ensure system resilience. In this research, we focus on Landmark Integration (LI) within the BEV domain to combine camera features and object detection labels with LiDAR features for robust and efficient detection. A standalone sensor system is limited by its capabilities, whereas a multi-sensor setup offers protection against failures of a single sensor. Exploiting the strengths of each sensor, our framework leverages cameras for high-resolution features within their limited receptive fields and, thanks to the properties of LiDAR, extends detection beyond the 100-meter mark where only non-camera sensors are typically effective. Evaluating our method on the nuScense dataset, our approach surpasses the camera-only baseline and, interestingly, even outperforms the perfect Sensor 2 by 2.4% AP, demonstrating the significant benefits of our method in improving detection capabilities.

A new approach for studying dissipative turbulence in liquid is presented, which is based on a simplified model of the range between the range of energy transfer and the dissipative range. This simplified model is the dissipative-range model of turbulence, which is the range of dissipative turbulence that is affected by the temperature of the liquid. A new dissipative thermal disturbance is introduced to capture the effect of temperature on the turbulence in a simplified way. This disturbance is the result of the interaction between a vorticity field and the compressibility of the liquid caused by its thermal expansion. A key feature of this disturbance is its ability to affect the flow in a non-uniform way, which is reflected in the distribution of the dissipative thermal disturbance in space. This disturbance also introduces the concept of dissipative thermal fluctuation, which is a new way to measure the effect of temperature on the turbulence in a simplified way. This new approach is validated by comparing it with direct numerical simulations of the turbulence in a simplified way. This study shows that the simplified model is capable of accurately predicting the dissipative thermal disturbance in a simplified way. This study also reveals that the dissipative thermal disturbance is responsible for a significant portion of the total dissipation of the liquid to a temperature-dependent level. This study demonstrates that the simplified model is capable of accurately predicting the total dissipation of the liquid to a temperature-dependent level. This study also reveals that the effect of temperature on the turbulence is significant in a simplified way. This study highlights

High-intensity lasers create complex self-diffraction patterns in liquid mediums due to the rapid heating of the focal point. Our study focuses on single-color lasers of 800 nm wavelength with energies up to a few microcoulombs, employing an analytical model to numerically calculate the thermal profile evolution within a liquid for these lasers. By considering the liquid's refractive index, our model takes into account the optical field amplitude and phase, as well as the dynamic changes resulting from electron delocalization and the Delocalization-Induced Optical Kerr Effect. Our findings reveal that the initial phase delay evolves in a non-linear and non-monotonic manner, with notable hotspots emerging at radii of 100-300 nm, corresponding to the locations of hot spots observed in interferograms. Moreover, our simulation of the delocalization-induced optical Kerr effect indicates that the thermal self-focusing effect is significantly enhanced at short timescales.

We analyze the CAdaP conversational design platform, which leverages natural language to assist designers in discovering platform capabilities, and extend it with automatic completion functionality. This capacity suggestion mechanism uses conversation context to analyze user queries and recommend appropriate platform capabilities. A approach combining deep learning with transformer neural networks, which draws on conversation history and user input, is used to provide suggested completions. This research focuses on maintaining consistency between training and testing data, employing Variational Autoencoders to encode conversation context, and representing unused capabilities as a distribution over relevant capabilities in the CAdaP use case setting. Experimental results, based on a real-world dialogue corpus, indicate that analyzing conversation history is crucial for effective task completion in design collaborations, and support the importance of maintaining consistency between conversation context in the communication and design assistance domains.

The study and analysis of data streams and records is a rapidly growing field, yet there's a lack of established frameworks for combining streaming and data analytics into unified pipelines. This research proposes a new framework, H-STREAM, that facilitates the creation of analytics pipelines by combining stream and data analytics into a unified environment, enabling end-to-end data processing and workflow management. The framework is built upon Apache Spark and includes a new language, H-STREAM, that generalizes data streaming and storage APIs to accommodate both streaming and data analytics operations. By providing a unified interface to analytics libraries and a shared data processing and scheduling layer, developers can create analytics pipelines using existing data analytics libraries, without needing to reimplement data streaming and storage logic. The paper also compares proposed implementation approaches and demonstrates the effectiveness of the framework through a case study that utilizes various data analytics libraries, such as Mahout, OpenCV, and NLTK.

The illustration technique is a powerful tool in quantum field theory calculations involving scattering processes at high energies. While widely applied in singular production scenarios, it is less commonly used in non-resonant situations at high energies. This study delves into non-resonant scattering cases for top quark associated vector boson production and compares current findings with existing research. The paper specifically focuses on distinguishing signatures of third generation fermions from fourth generation fermions and Higgs bosons in scenarios where a fourth generation exists. To this end, we compute and analyze differential cross sections for differential rates and establish comparison criteria for distinguishing between quantum field theories.

To overcome limitations in separate decoding and copying mechanisms, particularly when dealing with lengthy and complex input, this study introduces a unified replication mechanism for managing the outputs of SPARQL neural machine translation. It integrates the replication layer with the separate attention mechanism, allowing for precise control over when to replicate and non-replicate outputs, thus eliminating potential 'copying from the input' issues. Experiments conducted through adapting pre-trained general English-to-knowledge graph SPARQL models reveal the effectiveness of the proposed approach, outperforming the existing separate and rep-copying mechanisms and pushing the boundaries of knowledge graph neural machine translation capabilities.

This study offers the Venue Insights package to compute and compare citation related metrics based on author and venue profiles. A comprehensive analysis of the package functionality along with case studies comparing various metrics and benchmarks, such as the Packard Score versus the Iris Score, is provided. Additionally, this research explores alternative methods for evaluating research impact without relying on citation based metrics and considers the use of venue insights for this purpose.

Regulatory bodies' decisions have been heavily influenced by economic data analysis in the past, but now the capabilities of artificial intelligence models are being explored for such purposes. To introduce AI into the regulatory process, a need exists for a thorough examination of its economic model validation requirements. This is addressed by the paper, which discusses how traditional economic model validation principles can be applied to AI models to incorporate them into regulation. The traditional economic model validation framework is initially outlined, and then the paper examines the capabilities and limitations of existing AI methods in satisfying this validation process. This leads to the development of a novel AI model validation framework, with an emphasis on supervised learning models as a starting point. This work builds on previous research by Bertschek et al. and Lim et al. and provides a foundation for incorporating AI models into the regulatory process.

In numerous fields, hierarchical clustering is a widely used technique.  Standard
implementations typically model objects either directly through similarity matrices or indirectly using feature vectors.  Real-world observations often have parts that overlap, 
like images with boundaries and text with words and sentences. It's desirable to 
use information from observations to their advantage by grouping similar parts together 
to produce a hierarchy, while also utilizing information from similarity matrices or 
observation feature vectors as needed.  We present a novel, modular, and flexible hierarchical 
clustering method called "Fun-Fun Hierarchical Grouping with Overlaps" (Fun-HGO) that 
uses overlapping observations to produce a tree structure.  We demonstrate the utility of 
this approach in integrating feature and similarity information for applications like 
interpreting high-dimensional images and analyzing brain connectivity patterns.

Tensor decomposition, specifically the tensor ring format, has emerged as a powerful solution to complex recovery problems in various fields. A recent system designed for tensor ring restoration focuses on a fixed input image, which limits its effectiveness on live data such as video streams. To address this limitation, a new system is proposed that restores a tensor ring without interrupting data flow in real-time. This system is built upon a network architecture that can process individual data patches and is capable of using prior information from previous patches. To optimize performance, a patch monitoring approach is developed that allows the system to learn from the most relevant patch patterns. This system, named Patch Monitoring-based Streaming Tensor Ring Restoration, shows improved performance and efficiency, and is especially well-suited for applications requiring fast and continuous data processing, such as video streaming.

For any braided vector space $(V,c)$ within the category of braided groups $(V, c, \Gamma)$ with a finite braiding group, where $c$ acts diagonally on $V$, the associated Nichols algebra $\mathcal{B}(V,c)$ has been shown to have dimension either infinite or a specific $2\times 2$ Coxeter group order, as in [M-S]. This paper continues the exploration initiated in [M-S] by identifying two key cases where $\dim(\mathcal{B}(V,c))$ is finite, while demonstrating that one condition is necessary but not sufficient.

A recent breakthrough in theoretical work linked by Kolchinskii, Nazarov, and Vinogradov predicts a type of statistical behavior in complex wave systems during the early stages of chaos. This prediction suggests a hierarchy of spectral power levels, which we wanted to validate using computer simulations based on the original equations of motion. Our results show that these findings align closely with actual computer-generated solutions, confirming the theoretical model's accuracy and significance.

In the realm of finite graphs, the concept of standardization is crucial, where every graph can be transformed into a canonical form. A graph is considered standard if its automorphism group is maximally weighted relative to its edge adjacency matrix, implying that it cannot be changed anymore through the double coset method. Papers by Labahn and co-authors demonstrated that any finite graph can be simplified and showed that the number of possible reductions is maximally bounded by a polynomial scaled by a constant. Building upon these foundational studies, our analysis focuses on the single orbit scenario to derive a sequence of ordered transformations that results in a standardized graph, where each step represents a level of progression marked by an incrementally higher value of $t$, signifying the number of possible advancements.

This study investigates the thermodynamic properties of a monolayer graphene subject to a in-plane electrically-adjusted background. The single-electron energy spectrum was derived using the Dirac equation, and the thermodynamic characteristics were explored in the framework of random phase approximation (RPA). The response functions and excitation energies were calculated with reference to the bubble diagram, and the graphen's stability was analyzed in light of the Landau damping condition. The graphen's thermal behavior was further explored based on its thermodynamic potential. The findings reveal the influence of electrically-adjusted background and temperature on the thermodynamic characteristics and stability of the graphen. The results also show the occurrence of instability in the graphen's ground state due to the electrically-adjusted background in a specific energy-momentum region.

Our 115 MHz radio observations of the G-type flare star binary CR Draconis revealed significant single-sided modulation in its active B component. The brightness variations indicated electron-cyclotron maser radiation from the B component's magnetic pole. The beam width of the emission was estimated to be approximately 40 degrees, varying slightly with time. The brightness fluctuations could be attributed to the B component's rotation. A preliminary distance estimate placed the B component at around 1.2 astronomical units from its companion. The radio luminosity and period variations suggested the presence of a low-mass star in the binary system, with a possible mass of around 0.2-0.3 solar masses. The radio luminosity of the B component was comparable to that of the Sun during a flare cycle. The observed radio behavior of the B component suggested a more prolonged electron-cyclotron maser emission compared to other stellar systems. Further studies, including high-cadence optical observations and radial velocity measurements, could help to refine the binary system's parameters.

This study introduces ANR, a network designed to simulate human movement by
depicting virtual avatars with realistic motion. The primary objective of our
research is to develop virtual training environments with interactive elements.
The ANR model, consisting of an artificial neural network, defines articulated
avatar movements by using key joint angles as output data, with training
involving the network learning from position data. By integrating a self
organization mechanism for joint angle data, we ensure that generated movements
are physically plausible. Our results show that users perceive avatars created
with ANR to be in a stable state, and that these avatars produce consistent
movements when generating the same sequence of position data multiple times.
Building on top of UltraMotion, our work integrates ANR to create virtual human
movements that include interactions with the physical environment. By training 
the ANR model using position data that includes interactions, we demonstrate
its ability to generate dynamic movements that account for physical
interactions, including contact and non-contact forces.

This paper examines the complex interplay between human perception and intense modifications of images, focusing on how these modifications impact human vision and the design of machine vision algorithms. Human perception is influenced by factors such as noise, image compression, and intense filtering, prompting a need to understand how the brain adapts to these modifications. Meanwhile, machine vision models like convolutional neural networks are also affected by these intense modifications, raising questions about their reliability and robustness. We'll discuss key concepts and open challenges related to machine vision and its response to intense modifications, including image denoising and adversarial attacks, and highlight research gaps that remain to be filled.

The Chern-Simons theory when quantized in a specific way leads to a five-dimensional space, resulting in a key equation of q-deformed SU(4) and a complex associated algebra. Notably, a specific form of q-deformation, where q is a 14th root of unity, proves to be the most suitable for knot analysis. Applying this finding, the work demonstrates how to build rational invariants for a class of two-bridge knots from a specific algebraic framework, namely the Askey-Wilson algebra.

We have conducted an extensive study on the magnetic properties of two-dimensional systems consisting of triangular clusters linked together by weak interactions, using the full cluster quantum Monte Carlo method. The system is described by the following Hamiltonian, which takes into account magnetic interactions between different types of spins:

$\mathcal{H} = J_\textrm{S} \sum_{\sigma < \tau} \mathbf{S}_\sigma \cdot \mathbf{S}_\tau + J_\textrm{C} \sum_{\sigma, \tau} \mathbf{S}_\sigma \cdot \mathbf{S}_\tau + H_\textrm{C}$.

The first term in the Hamiltonian accounts for interactions between square lattice spins, while the second term represents the interactions between triangular cluster spins. The parameter $H_\textrm{C}$ ensures that the total magnetization remains fixed.

We have analyzed the system's behavior in the regime where the ratio of triangular to square spin interactions is less than 0.2, and found that the critical temperature is almost linearly dependent on this ratio.

Additionally, we have investigated the response of the system to an external magnetic field along the trigonal axis.

The results of our study reveal that the system exhibits a complex interplay between the square and triangular spin interactions, which gives rise to an antiferromagnetic state below the critical temperature, characterized by an in-plane

The effectiveness of zero-shot performance of pre-trained language models in the education sector is hindered by their inadequate alignment with educational language, which is a combination of specialized jargon and simplified expressions. To overcome this limitation, we suggest a two-part approach consisting of dataset assembly and fine-tuning a language model to adjust its textual representations to better suit educational needs. This leads to improved learning outcomes across a wide range of tasks. To identify the most suitable datasets for tuning our language model, we employ a novel, pre-trained model-based ranking system. Furthermore, our proposed ensemble approach, which combines several datasets, significantly outperforms the results obtained by training on a single dataset. Ultimately, our results demonstrate that zero-shot performance on the education sector can be optimized by adjusting a general-purpose language model to better fit its language and context.

In the $Z_3$-symmetric extension of the MSSM known as the NMSSM, we examine the electroweak phase transition (EWPT) to understand its potential for producing a first-order phase transition and generate gravitational waves. We initially analyzed the EWPT under various $Y, \lambda_1, \lambda_2, \lambda_3$ and $m_{H_1^0}, m_{H_2^0}, m_{H_3^0}$ scenarios, with the EWPO model serving as a baseline with $\lambda_1 = 0.1$ and $\lambda_2 = 0.1$. We then explored the impact of varying the $Y$ parameter and incorporating a general CP-violation into the $V_{H_1^0}$ term in the potential. We also investigated how LHC and dark matter searches constrain the $Z_3$-symmetric extension of the MSSM, specifically by examining how variations in the $Y$ parameter affect the constraints and detection prospects for future high-luminosity LHC runs. We discovered that, unlike in other models, parameters in the $V_{H_1^0}$ term in the EWPO model are tightly constrained, with constraints on $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$ being comparable to or even stricter than those from the SM Higgs mass measurement at the LHC, respectively. We introduce an innovative tool for accurately identifying robust millimeter-wave spectroscopic redshifts in distant galaxies. The High-z Sudoku diagnostic involves generating multiple $k$-band (8-13 $\mu$m) Sudoku spectra, by randomly sampling millimeter-wave galaxy spectra, and examining their corresponding Sudoku patterns. By comparing these simulated spectra with observed spectra and calculating the proportion of instances where the redshifts match, we develop the High-z Sudoku diagnostic ratio ($DR_{HS}$). The $DR_{HS}$ metric provides insight into the reliability of millimeter-wave spectroscopic redshifts, particularly at z > 3-4. We introduce a new method for calculating $DR_{HS}$ ratios, which leverages observed single-epoch spectra, eliminating the need for computationally intensive multi-epoch observations. This approach offers a reliable and efficient means of assessing the robustness of redshift measurements without introducing significant biases.

Using the time-of-flight method with ultracold 39K atoms, a study was conducted on the $S=1/2$ Heisenberg antiferromagnetic lattice on a triangular structure. Near the half-fingernail state in the magnetic field, the researchers observed the restoration of the $C_2$ symmetry, but outside this region, they found evidence of a first-order transition with simultaneous destruction of the $C_2$ symmetry and formation of the liquid state. The coexistence of the $C_2$-restored and liquid states was interpreted as resulting from the merging of the $C_2$-restored state with the liquid phase. The researchers also discovered that the order parameter in the magnetic field and the spatial distribution of the charge in the liquid state exhibit a logarithmic dependence on the magnetic field intensity. The findings confirm the existence of the $C_2$-broken and liquid states in the lattice and provide a precise description of the ground state. The study used the spin dynamics simulation to compare experimental results with theoretical predictions.

Our research focuses on understanding the interplay between the confinement and chiral symmetry-breaking phases in non-Abelian Yang--Mills theory with matter fields in the fundamental representation. Specifically, we explore the role of the number of flavors, Nf, in a scenario where mass is generated through a potential that is flat in the absence of a positive mass term. By conducting simulations in a range of dimensions and temperatures, we identified a distinct transition marked by a significant increase in the susceptibility of the relevant scalar field, which signals the transition from confinement to deconfinement. Furthermore, we analyzed the role of a marginally irrelevant operator near the transition point and found that its beta function can be accurately described by a scaling dimension that depends on Nf in a gauge-invariant manner.

Cr2Al, a compound with the tetragonal I4/mmm structure, has been discovered to exhibit complex magnetic ordering as the temperature is reduced.
Our studies have shown that the Cr atoms within this material are arranged in an antiferromagnetic pattern along the c-axis, with a particular transition occurring at 270 K and at 190 K where the magnetic structure changes significantly.
Magnetization experiments under an external field indicate a significant temperature-dependent shift in the Cr2Al material, displaying a distinct change at 270 K and exhibiting ferromagnetic-like behavior at low temperatures.
Cr54, a long-lived Cr isotope, has been found to emit a gamma-ray spectrum of two peaks at 91.7 keV and 122.1 keV when the material is in its magnetic state.
Additionally, our data has shown that the magnetic field has a significant influence on the material's hyperfine structure, with an in-plane direction along the a-axis being identified through examination of the magnetic pattern.
We have also found that the exchange interaction between the Cr atoms is predominantly affected by a single crystal field and that its strength is significantly lower than that of another similar material, with the ratio being 0.12 to 0.13 times smaller.

An enhanced kinetic equation, where the collision frequency changes with the velocity of particles, effectively models rarefied gas dynamics and is especially useful for near-equilibrium states. This new framework shows promising potential for studying complex intermolecular potential influences on such flows, which is difficult to achieve using traditional methods like the Navier-Stokes-Fokker-Planck equation. We applied it to polyatomic rarefied gases and to models involving energy and angular momentum transfer, including a coarse-grained version of the VRA model. A key finding was that this new framework accurately reproduces the velocity-dependent collision frequency and its relationship with temperature fluctuations resulting from different gas interaction potentials.

We've developed a method for creating semantic interpreters that require minimal training data and can be easily adapted to various contexts without needing to know more about their underlying knowledge systems. To accomplish this, we utilize pre-trained language models to create a compact, efficient model capable of performing semantic interpretation. We demonstrate that this approach works effectively on two challenging knowledge bases, namely ConceptNet and DALI, showing comparable performance to state-of-the-art models trained on vast datasets. Moreover, we find that this method is particularly suitable for deployment on devices with limited resources, such as mobile devices, due to its small size and high efficiency.

The future Electron-Iron Collider will be the world's largest particle accelerator when it becomes operational in 2025. Its primary purpose is to investigate the fundamental components of the universe, consisting of protons and neutrons, to gain insight into their underlying structure. To achieve this, the collider will need to track numerous fast-moving particles resulting from high-energy, ultra-boosted collisions to accurately reconstruct the events. To meet these demanding requirements, researchers have been making significant advancements in silicon tracking sensors, specifically using thin silicon layers with high resistance and low growth temperatures, coupled with specialized readout integrated circuits featuring advanced technology. Recent breakthroughs in developing and testing these sensors have been made, and the current state of the technology, along with the future directions needed to advance the project, will be thoroughly examined.

We've discovered a variable nucleus in a low-mass active galaxy called NGC 4449, where recent high-resolution X-ray observations from Chandra revealed periodic fluctuations. The light changes appear every 22.8 seconds with variations in amplitude of around 0.3. Our analysis of past data from XMM-Newton and the Swift-BAT catalog revealed further activity, where the X-ray fluctuations increased to around 0.6, indicating the presence of X-ray state transitions. The observed periodicity aligns with the mass of the supermassive black hole at around $10^6 M_\odot$, suggesting that the black hole might possess a low-mass disk consisting of soft X-rays, where thermal oscillations occur. However, the variability in the X-ray state could also be attributed to the presence of corona flares or other outbursts.

Observing the radial magnetic field in HD58260 is complicated by its extremely low surface brightness and high noise levels in existing spectropolarimetric measurements. A promising approach to studying such stars is by analyzing specific spectral lines under non-local thermodynamic equilibrium (NLTE) conditions. In this context, a two-level atom model is used to simulate the behavior of Fe I and Ca I lines under various magnetic field configurations. By comparing simulated and observed spectral lines, it is found that the star's atmosphere exhibits a significant variation in radial magnetic field strength with an average field strength of about 80 Gauss and a maximum field strength of about 130 Gauss. A key advantage of the two-level atom model is its ability to accurately model certain spectral features, such as the reverse polarization of Ca I 617.2 nm and the asymmetric polarization of Fe I 615.0 nm, that are not well-explained by more traditional models.

A novel expression for the Dunkl operator is introduced and demonstrated to have some desirable characteristics in one dimension, such as the Dunkl transformation preserving the $H_{\alpha}$-Gaussian measure on $\mathbb{R}^{+}$. This has led to the conclusion that the Dunkl operator's $L^{p}(h_{\alpha})\rightarrow L^{p}(h_{\alpha})$ mapping property holds for $1\leq p\leq \infty$. Additionally, the expression is employed to prove an inequality involving the $L^{p}(h_{\alpha })$ norm and its relation to the classical Gaussian inequality for $1\leq p\leq \infty$.

A young and unusual blue compact galaxy, NGC 5253, has been extensively researched,
revealing multiple starburst regions within a relatively small area. The challenge
in understanding NGC 5253's star formation history arises from the presence of two
distinct starburst regions formed within a short time frame. By utilizing ALMA's
H24$\alpha$ and H30$\alpha$ line observations, we have analyzed starburst region I's
newly formed stars, focusing particularly on the H30$\alpha$ line's ability to
detect the most massive stars. Our study of NGC 5253's starburst region I has shown
that the H30$\alpha$ line's emission is closely related to the presence of O-type
stars, with a correlation of 90% or more. The H24$\alpha$ and H30$\alpha$ line
continuum emissions have also been found to be related to dust emission, with a
correlation of approximately 90%. By analyzing the H30$\alpha$ line's emission
pattern, we have identified a correlation between line intensity and dust mass,
suggesting that star formation occurs in a manner consistent with other galaxies.
