A measure-preserving action of a countable group on a probability space is considered to be measure-preserving. Constant orbit equivalence stiffness for such actions was defined as a property where any measure-preserving equivalence between orbits can be broken down into a combination of original action and another action, provided the original action satisfies specific conditions. This concept is related to coarse geometry, specifically coarse stiffness, in the context of group actions. The aim of this study is to develop theories of coarse stiffness for group actions with invariance of domain by constant. The study shows that hyperbolic lattice group actions are coarse equivalence-stiff for virtualy cotic group actions and explores the possibility of developing a similar theory for virtually polycyclic group actions.

This study examines the estimation of conditional expectation functions, specifically with regard to a dependent variable of interest, in relation to multiple independent variables, one of which is binary and the other is continuous. By collecting survey data through a rotating panel design that includes an interconnected sampling process across multiple stages, researchers can gather insights from multiple cohorts over time, sharing the underlying population in common. Leveraging this dataset, our approach combines two key methods to achieve more accurate results, with the goal of achieving a significant reduction in bias estimates and enhanced nonparametric efficiency. As a result, our simulations demonstrate a substantial decrease in bias, with corresponding enhancements in finite sample mean square error performance, specifically when sampling from a large population. The biases associated with our estimator are also shown to converge at a faster rate, at $O(T^{-1/4}N^{-1/4})$, achieving superior asymptotic performance, when sampling from a large, fixed population as the time period and cross-sectional size tend towards infinity.

The spread of highly contagious diseases like SARS-CoV-2 has led to significant societal and economic challenges, prompting a need for timely estimates of the current infection rates to guide public health decisions. Building upon previous research, this study develops and evaluates an observer-based approach to estimate the current new infections and recoveries based on historical data from reported cases. By applying least-squares optimization to estimate model parameters, we can improve the accuracy of these estimates and provide more effective guidance for vaccination strategies and quarantine policies. Numerical simulations demonstrate the efficacy of this approach in capturing the complex dynamics of the coronavirus pandemic, particularly during the recent waves in Brazil.

Recent advances in temporal knowledge graphs (TKGs) have led to improved prediction of event dynamics and attributes. Tarek et. al's report highlights that most existing methods for TKGs involve using random neural network initialization and then optimizing the model's parameters to achieve better performance. Conversely, this paper argues that random initialization can be replaced with a fixed model for TKGs, yielding superior performance without the need for parameter optimization. Moreover, this approach can be applied to both TKGs and their static counterparts. To validate this hypothesis, a new algorithm based on RNN is proposed, utilizing a fixed GRU for TKGs in place of the traditional parameter optimization method. The proposed approach achieves remarkable results on two standard datasets - CW and ST-100 - outperforming existing methods by margins of 4% and 6% respectively.

This study focuses on creating a single, comprehensive geometric model of Kerr-lens mode-locking (SLM-KK) to swiftly and effectively analyze ML-kickers in various types of resonators. Employing a geometric representation, researchers can assess whether an optical resonator is suitable for Kerr-lens mode-locking without conducting in-depth beam simulations. These resonator classifications are based on the resonator's geometric properties, and a study examines the applicability of these categories to commonly used resonator types. By categorizing Kerr lenses into three types (converging, diverging, and non-active) and resonators into groups (g-parameter based or mirror curvature configurations), researchers can establish general principles for implementing ML-kickers in different setups. This approach is particularly useful for non-confocal four-mirror telescopes and other complex resonator configurations. By applying this analysis, researchers can identify potential issues with existing designs, such as unstable cavity modes, and provide insights into suitable mirror configurations that avoid these problems. Ultimately, this analytical method aims to facilitate quick and effective evaluation of Kerr-lens mode-locking in various resonator setups.

Online learning methods have been widely used to process large datasets, especially when resources are limited. Recent advancements in distributed online algorithms have enabled training on multiple devices while minimizing wireless communication costs. However, these distributed online algorithms are sensitive to hardware variations, which can cause performance disparities. Moreover, they are not designed to adapt dynamically to changing computational capabilities. This study aims to address this issue by developing an asynchronous online federated learning framework that can efficiently utilize multiple devices. By incorporating a novel federated additive stochastic gradient descent algorithm, the proposed framework reduces communication costs, takes into account device heterogeneity, and generates adaptable delay compensation. Experimental results on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate its improved convergence rate, lower communication costs, and enhanced robustness compared to state-of-the-art approaches.

We have investigated how a three-dimensional photonic crystal back reflector affects the absorption of light in various thin layers of silicon. Using advanced modeling, we have calculated how this back reflector enhances absorption of light for different thicknesses. Our experiments show that for a 500 to 1000 nanometer thick silicon layer, and particularly a 50 nanometer ultrathin layer, the photonic crystal enhances absorption of light significantly, achieving nearly 100% efficiency in the former and a 2.5-fold increase in the latter. Moreover, our research indicates that photonic crystals broaden the range of light absorption beyond what can be achieved with other types of back reflectors through a novel 3D light trapping effect. These findings can lead to the development of new types of thin and ultrathin photovoltaic devices that can work more efficiently.

This paper formulates and gives preliminary explanations for the asymptotic behaviors of tetration and superfunctions when the underlying function is multivalued, under the condition that the principal value of the primary function is employed in its definition. The proposed hypotheses arise from the consideration of particular cases of the asymptotic expansions of the asymptotic powers series and the asymptatic logarithmic towers.

High dimensional expansions, such as tensor products and high order local systems, have greatly advanced our understanding of high dimensional phenomena, particularly in combinatorics. Recently, a more general framework was proposed, encompassing all such expansions and allowing for their independent constructions. This proof, although existence-based, lacks explicit constructions. We challenge this absence by creating a universal method for constructing high dimensional expansions in a specific, yet intricate, scenario. Specifically, our work demonstrates an expansion equivalent in size to a generalized local search algorithm, reminiscent of a 1987 paper by Wigderson. Furthermore, our construction has the additional benefit of preserving group symmetry, particularly for the symmetric group.

Our investigation into the crystal GdInO3 reveals an unexpected magnetic structure. Initially, the Gd ions display long, thin antiferromagnetic order using the Wooster configuration, and this order is then substituted by a shorter, thicker antiferromagnetic order using the Yafet-Kitvel configuration as the magnetic field is raised. Furthermore, our research shows that the magnetic properties of GdInO3 are highly anisotropic, exhibiting a notable increase in magnetization when the field is applied parallel to the ab plane compared to when it is applied perpendicular to this plane. These magnetic attributes can be successfully explained through a combination of superexchange and single ion anisotropy in the magnetic properties of the Gd ions.

The challenge of link prediction in large-scale network analysis is significant, particularly when dealing with sparse graph structures. Traditional methods, focused on node embeddings, have been ineffective in capturing node connections in sparse graphs. Our research presents a new approach, sparse self-stacking neural network embeddings, for accurately predicting links in such structures. This approach utilizes self-stacking neural networks and sparse self-assembly to produce embeddings that accurately reflect node connections. Our experiments on seven real-world network datasets confirm the superiority of our method, sparse SSNE, over existing embedding methods, both sparse and dense. Notably, our findings show that sparse SSNE outperforms other approaches in predicting links within these large-scale sparse graph structures.

Highly advanced nano-fabrication techniques have been used to create a type of chamber from a specific class of materials, referred to as deep silicon VCSELs. Silicon-based vapor chambers have previously undergone thermal testing to confirm their operational capabilities. Leveraging deep silicon processing capabilities allows for the creation of extremely compact vapor chambers with significant implications for miniaturized atomic devices, potentially enabling widespread integration with silicon-based photonic technologies.

This study investigates the non-linear distortion power of dual-polarization 4D-FFT, a modulation scheme employed in 5G new radio integrated circuits. By considering the interaction between dual-polarization and 4D-FFT in both time and frequency domains, a comprehensive analytical model for power consumption is developed for single single-carrier 4D-FFT with unequal protection levels for polarization. The model accounts for the complex power consumption of multiple single-carrier 4D-FFT systems with diverse protected levels used in massive access communications. When the protection levels are uniform, a simplified single single-carrier 4D-FFT model can be utilized. The findings from this model were validated through Monte Carlo simulations.

We introduce a Deep Learning-based method called FIRe-GAN that leverages visible and infrared sensors to generate highly realistic images of wildfires in near real-time. By leveraging dual camera feeds, our approach enhances the fidelity of generated fire imagery compared to using a single source. The method employs two adversarial networks, one for each modality, combined with an additional variational autoencoder, to ensure accurate image synthesis and capture the inherent characteristics of the input data. The proposed technique is evaluated through comprehensive quantitative metrics, such as the Fréchet Inception Score, as well as expert human evaluation, demonstrating its superior performance. The FIRe-GAN model is available for download at https://github.com/abdelrahman-ahmed/ FIRe-GAN.

Detecting signs of depression on the internet has the potential to aid those experiencing this common and often long-lasting condition by providing timely support and early intervention. Past research has primarily focused on developing computational models, using techniques like natural language processing and machine learning to analyze online text and detect indicators of depression, including discussions of physical and emotional symptoms as well as suicidal thoughts. Our research contributes to this area by developing a dataset consisting of 10,000 social media posts from individuals experiencing physical and emotional symptoms associated with depression, drawn from an online community for antidepressant discussion. Our study outlines how we gathered and processed this data, along with our initial exploration of how it compares to other datasets in the field.

Building on earlier work, a random graphical model is created to depict the spread of COVID-19 within a population divided into communities. A specific subset of this population is considered infectious, and the model focuses primarily on this subset along with those who come into contact with them. The expected size of these communities and the total population within the model's network are calculated and analyzed. The model also explores the variability in its key parameters and discusses the impact of community boundaries on the spread of the virus.

Using the Gogny-Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov method along with the Random Phase Approximation, the nuclear responses of $^{24}$Mg and $^{28}$Si to inelastic scattering of $^{12}$C at 60 MeV are investigated. Particular focus is given to the effects of coupling between isoscalar monopole and quadrupole modes, particularly in the context of prestrained deformation. Our calculations reveal that taking into account the coupling significantly improves agreement with experimental data, especially in the case of $^{28}$Si, where it yields a notably different isoscalar monopole resonance energy compared to the Lip诺v parameter. The work underscores the significance of the coupling between collective modes in shaping nuclear properties and underscores the need for a deeper understanding of collective motion in both deformed and nondeformed nuclei.

This study examines the stability of stick-slip systems with Coulomb friction, regulated through feedback control. To achieve this, a general dynamical system is developed to capture the unique properties of stick-slip and stable convergence, along with inequalities that identify both convergence rates and the stability of limit sets. To validate the applicability of these theoretical findings, two distinct models with Coulomb friction are analyzed: the Van der Pol oscillator with the control theory's sliding mode mechanism and the piezoelectric actuator, featuring the physics-based study of friction.

Reinforcement learning faces significant challenges in handling risky situations. While risk-aware methods like risk-sensitive policy gradients and risk-aversion techniques have been explored, they often struggle to adapt to dynamic environments or produce optimal results. This paper introduces the first risk management framework grounded in Bellman principles. By incorporating an explicit action-level risk factor into traditional Bellman equations, our approach enables end-to-end learning for simultaneous risk-aware policy and value function training. We demonstrate the efficacy of PropRFBM, a proposed risk framework based on this concept, using a newly created testbed for risk-sensitive reinforcement learning. Empirical evaluations reveal that PropRFBM enables agents to efficiently balance risk and performance in complex, risky environments comparable to real-world scenarios.

Recommenders utilizing sequential algorithms often leverage observation sequences to predict subsequent items, which researchers argue effectively tap into user intent. However, there's a notable limitation: these recommender systems lack explicit user intent representations. This absence makes them incapable of explaining predicted items and limits their ability to adapt to shifts in user preferences when encountering new items. To mitigate this issue, we've developed a groundbreaking three-step framework, the Hidden User Intent (HUI) framework, that explicitly models and explains user intent. In the first step, we represent intent as a latent variable and estimate its parameters using maximum likelihood methods. Next, we incorporate these parameters as a regularisation term in the next-item prediction process. Finally, we reframe the predicted next item as an observation resulting from both user intent and an action error component. By applying this framework to an item-succession based recommender system, we demonstrate its effectiveness in both explaining recommended items and adapting to user preference changes. Furthermore, we extend the approach to next-set prediction and confirm its efficacy through theoretical and empirical analyses.

The solvable double confluent Heun equation is generalized from previous research, establishing a specific form of the solvable double confluent Heun operator with symmetric coefficients. When specific conditions are applied to potential parameters, this operator transforms into the Ablowitz-Kaup-Radwick-Furse equation with a rational solution of any order. Additionally, we propose a new method to analyze the fundamental solutions of the double confluent Heun equation, involving a systematic unfolding of the outset solution space near the critical point at infinity.

Theoretical bounds for linear output-prediction problems involving matrix data have been extensively studied and derived.  For consistent theoretical bounds, the following conditions are assumed: sufficient pre-knowledge of relevant structure and variability within matrix components and the input variable.  However, in practical scenarios, such information is often lacking.  Consequently, the input variable and matrix components can be heterogeneous, and there may be no association between the target variable and the input variable.  To address these limitations, we derive new lower bounds for the mean squared error of a matrix's single column vector under heterogeneous, but structured, conditions.  We explore the impact of incorporating symmetries and other structural constraints on the target variable and matrix, as well as the influence of group heterogeneity.  We start by considering the case where the target variable and matrix components are drawn from multiple sub-populations and show that under group heterogeneity, we cannot expect a negative expected prediction error.  Instead, we examine the minimum possible prediction error, achieved when the group means are associated with the input variable.  To make these bounds more applicable, we derive more relaxed versions, which rely on the assumption of input variable homogeneity, and compare the new bounds to existing work on target variable symmetry and covariance structure.  For the case where the group means are unknown, we provide theoretical bounds, which take into account the symmetry of matrices, and compare these with previous results.  To illustrate the new bounds, we use a data set from a

The theoretical essential topological representation was proposed and demonstrated using the scalar field as an example. A model was created that incorporates the essential projector without relying on symmetry, allowing for the description of an arbitrary number of zero-mode states. The mathematical framework was developed that connects this mathematical model to a physical system of a meson cloud surrounding a baryon. This approach resolves the inherent problem of non-orthogonal zero-mode states by using a matrix of overlap between these states. Additionally, this colorless construction avoids the necessity of color degrees of freedom.

This study, including the latest data from the LHCb and CMS collaborations, reveals an inconsistency in the ratio of semi-inclusive to inclusive lepton-flavor Equivalence, which relies on the ratio of muonic to electronic differential decay rates in $B\to V\ell^+\ell^-$ decays. The ratio, analyzed across various $q^2$ intervals, exhibits a discrepancy in the $B\to J/\psi$ case, specifically in the low $q^2$ range, and our analysis indicates this could be attributed to model-independent isospin corrections. The study further discusses potential experimental factors that could influence this observation.

This paper presents a novel, decentralized architecture termed DecoNet, along with a distributed control approach allowing its use in a wide variety of interconnected systems, known as Multi-channel Networks (MCNs). For DecoNet to function seamlessly in such networks it must meet two criteria: firstly, it should automatically adapt to any suitable network configuration without requiring manual recalibration of its parameters; and secondly, it should be easily integrated without the need for extensive modifications to its existing structure. In order to meet these criteria, the proposed architecture is entirely distributed, allowing it to be applied to any network with a specific communication structure, as long as controllers can access information regarding lower triangular and diagonal system matrices; controllers for non-diagonal system matrices, in turn, should have access to the complete system state. Notably, this requirement is less restrictive than traditional centralized approaches, which typically necessate knowledge of the entire system state. By evaluating its capabilities using a simulation setup, the proposed architecture is shown to facilitate the stable integration of new, independent subsystems without the need for re-tuning existing controllers, a crucial aspect of modern network design.

The COVID19 outbreak is a major global event that has had far-reaching consequences on the world economy, society, and daily routines. The rapid dissemination of information about the pandemic has led to the spread of misinformation and negative news, which can significantly impact the spread of the virus. The significant amount of news data available presents an ideal opportunity to monitor the public's response and behavior. A novel feature to be proposed in this research is the classification of COVID19-related news into two categories: 'before vaccination' and 'after vaccination'. A novel BERT model, pre-trained using news data and fine-tuned for this purpose, will demonstrate the most effective performance in classifying these news sources into the proposed categories. The model's effectiveness will be evaluated and it will be shown to outperform other models.

This article examines the influence of edge weights and their associated modeling methods on recent network studies. We examine the underlying reasoning for choosing a specific weight type (binary vs different vs positive significant vs binary with signs) and introduce diverse ways to represent these weights. We also discuss suitable distance and similarity measures for each and survey a range of network analysis applications, along with the existing literature, that utilize weighted networks.

The study of eco-evolutionary dynamics has seen various approaches emerge to analyze how ecological and evolutionary changes interact and influence one another. This paper examines the timeframes of eco-evolutionary dynamics, ranging from the deep past to the present, and identifies the factors that regulate their speed. Key factors include the forces of natural and sexual selection, as evidenced in a basic model of cyclical, co-occurring changes between species, which reveals that evolutionary changes are often more rapid than anticipated. This finding holds true in multiple systems, and our research indicates that when a species' ecological and evolutionary changes interact and affect each other, their rates may be amplified. This may be especially true in cases of rapid, cyclic, and interdependent changes between species, and suggests that the effect of environment-evolution feedback loops on evolutionary change may exceed expectations.

Current research on self-supervised learning for speech has shown its effectiveness in improving speech recognition performance, with recent findings indicating that its benefits extend to anti-spam detection tasks as well. To better understand its educative and anti-agonistic vulnerabilities, a controlled study was conducted involving over 10,000 speakers who modified their voices using text-to-speech technology, which is designed to disguise speech identity. The largest controlled study of its kind so far, it revealed that self-supervised models are vulnerable to manipulated voices, with performance dropping significantly under certain levels of synthesis. Notably, performance degradation was more pronounced than in comparable supervised experiments. To counter this, a novel defense mechanism, which incorporates spectral noise, was developed and tested, showing a notable increase in accuracy under heavily synthesized voices.

The Embrace of Distributed Digital Platforms reshapes existing market structures, facilitating seamless connectivity and interoperability of digital assets and services. The integration of the Embrace Layer leverages the power of distributed ledger technology, empowering a decentralized hub that leverages digital tokens to facilitate the fluidity of money, goods, and services. The Embrace Layer's innovation in digital interconnectivity is set to transform the traditional exchange model, with significant implications for financial markets, central exchanges, and regulatory frameworks.

In epidemiological research, missing data is a common issue. Our approach involves creating a function that gauges the impact of assumptions made to address missing data on study outcomes by considering a range of potential scenarios. In the context of the Exposure Assessment Sensitivity Evaluation (EASE) initiative, a new tool called the E-value has been developed to quantify the influence of potential biases arising from absent data. The mechanism behind the E-value is similar to that of the Z-value, which has been widely used in the missing data literature for a long time. Our method is based on Bayesian analysis and can be applied to both binary and continuous outcomes in various study designs, such as case-control and cohort studies. Our approach also extends to the analysis of multiple outcomes in line with the principles of partial multiplicity. Our findings demonstrate that the E-value can effectively assess the effect of plausible scenarios on research conclusions in real-world studies.

The quantum plane $\mathbb{C}[x,y]$ over the field $\mathbb{C}(q^{-1})$ has a specific group of $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ symmetries, which is the focus of this letter. A prior study by Bidi and MacIsaac was simplified and built upon in this work, which provides a more extensive and accessible overview, incorporating additional features such as dependencies on q, the use of a reduced relevant subalgebra, and allowing for arbitrary values of q.

The ever-connected vehicle is becoming integral to our lives, with responsibilities extending beyond road safety to include traffic management, emergency response, and disaster relief. The federated education standard widely adopted by the automotive industry enables vehicle systems to learn about each other, although privacy concerns persist despite system capabilities. Internet of Vehicles and Blockchain technologies have been developed to address this issue, with this paper presenting a comprehensive review of research leveraging these technologies to address vehicle federation issues. Following an in-depth analysis of existing research, we identify that the proposed solutions effectively address several challenges in vehicle federation, with particular emphasis on the need for an integrated framework to implement Internet of Vehicles and Blockchain technologies as recommended by industry experts.

Measurements of charged hadron jet properties are presented for proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 5.02 TeV, recorded by the ATLAS detector at the LHC. The jets were reconstructed using the anti-$k_t$ algorithm with a radius parameter of 0.4. The jets were correlated with bottom quark fragmentation, identified through the reconstruction of $\mu$ + $\mathcal{D}$ final states, containing at least one secondary vertex with three tracks originating from a B-hadron decay, resulting in the production of direct Fries, those produced through the decay of B-hadrons, and both types of production. The results of the study indicate that in both production types, the charged particle fuese distribution exhibits an enhancement in the high fuese region above the NLO-predicted prediction, while being in agreement with the prediction in the low fuese region. The findings are compared to predictions from Monte Carlo models.

The growing demand for MQS research and quantum computing tools has led to an increase in collaboration between the quantum science community and various research institutions, as well as an effort to reduce the cost of accessing MQS platforms.  As a result, various research facilities have been developed to provide quantum science and technology platforms at significantly reduced costs.  In this paper, we introduce a new MQS research platform located at the Fermilab Quantum Information and Computing Center (QICC) in Chicago, IL, USA, which is equipped with 50 millikelvin-temperature computers and networked connectivity to facilitate collaboration.  In addition, the platform includes an on-site fabrication and repair center, as well as training and educational resources for the quantum science and technology community.  With its unique combination of features, the QICC platform aims to support quantum science and technology research initiatives at Fermilab, as well as in broader academic and corporate organizations.

This research paper focuses on identifying and understanding misuses of cryptocurrencies within the cryptocurrency ecosystem. To date, there has been a scarcity of studies on actual market abuses in the cryptocurrency domain. This study is the first to thoroughly examine and categorize market abuses from a program analysis standpoint. To facilitate discussions on preventing such abuses, we conducted a detailed analysis of the root causes and consequences associated with them. Furthermore, we conducted a survey involving 10 participants to gauge awareness and knowledge regarding market abuse among the cryptocurrency community. Our survey revealed that many users are unaware of their accounts being compromised, and many developers lack the knowledge or tools to detect or prevent such abuses. To address this gap, we propose potential solutions, including community-driven educational initiatives, open-source detection tools, and the creation of a shared database of malicious cryptocurrencies. We believe that implementing these best practices will ultimately minimize the severity of market abuses within the cryptocurrency domain.

Automatically categorizing people in videos without any labeled data can significantly enhance various vision tasks. Most existing methods rely on pre-trained models, using either visual cues or a combination of visual cues and natural language processing techniques. However, these approaches have limitations, such as only working with specific categories or requiring extensive manual labeling. A novel approach called Web-scraped Category-Aware Word Tagging (WebCawt) was proposed to address these challenges by automatically generating a large-scale tagging dataset based on the assumptions that the required visual concepts are commonly searched on the web and that people use language to describe what they see. A new large-scale tagging dataset, called Wuhan Ongoing Real-time Tagging Hub (WORTH), was introduced, consisting of 1000 video clips from everyday urban scenes. An algorithm was developed to automatically extract visual categories from people's verbal feedback in real-time, leveraging a neural network model for visual classification and a dictionary of natural language phrases.

This study proposes a sparse reconstruction seismic imaging approach using proximal mean networks to solve the seismic imaging inverse problem. The proposed approach combines the proximal mean network with the generalized Gaussian potential to develop a new non-convex sparse regularization method, which is effective for handling noises and outliers in geophysical data with large amplitude. The proximal mean network maps the sparse coefficients to the data's amplitude, and its training is performed using the alternating direction method of multipliers, making it a practical tool for sparse seismic imaging. The proposed approach also includes numerical experiments and an application to a real seismic dataset, demonstrating its effectiveness and robustness compared to the L1 norm and the SCARLET prior.

In this context, the semigroups of composition operators are examined, focusing on their influence on the BMOA space and its variants. Their effect on the norm and weak*-topology is specifically analyzed. Additionally, the research extends to the integral operators, examining which ones preserve the properties of BMOA and a subset known as VMOA.

Within the large-$N$ Haagerup model, we study how operator insertions at the core of a circular strip affect the overlap of wavefunctions when periodicity is disrupted. It is found that these corrections lead to significant universal deviations in the surface free energy, characterized by universal coefficients. Furthermore, these findings are applicable to other systems exhibiting Haagerup-like model characteristics.

Historical collections hold invaluable insights into past languages, yet their extensive scope poses significant challenges for analysis. We propose an innovative approach to accurately categorize historically derived texts into their part-of-speech groups by employing a test-set split strategy and machine learning. This involves dividing a corpus into familiar and unknown sections by randomly allocating up to 30% of the data to the unfamiliar set. We then develop a forecasting model to predict the part-of-speech group distribution of the unfamiliar set based on the familiar set's labeling. To further refine our results, we employ a post-processing step to adapt the predicted distributions. Our experiments on annotated texts from 19th and 20th centuries reveal that our approach outperforms traditional machine learning methods, with a notable improvement of up to 10% in F1-score accuracy.

Integrals of polynomially bounded functions that are non-smooth can be challenging to compute due to their lack of continuity. To address this issue, we are establishing a more robust framework for interaction energies and forces in mathematical physics, and for the treatment of a measure of non-smoothness in image processing. Our approach involves two key steps: first, we are proving interaction energy principles for a space with a non-smooth structure, and second, we are extending these principles to functions with non-smooth structures, including those with discontinuities. Our methodology involves the use of Gamma-convergence, and we are leveraging the work of De Giorgi to derive these results. Our findings have significant implications for the treatment of non-smooth interaction energies and forces, as well as for the development of a convex model in total variation denoising. Our work also provides a rigorous foundation for the analysis of non-smooth functions with a measure of non-smoothness p-differential structure, p≥2.

The design of safety-critical systems, such as those in automotive systems, 
poses significant challenges due to their intricate specifications. 
These complex systems, characterized by numerous interactions and complex 
requirements, make it difficult to define their specifications accurately. 
To alleviate this burden, our innovation lies in a pioneering assistant, designed 
to streamline the conversion process from user input in a familiar format 
to precise formal specifications. This assistant leverages a knowledge base 
of common expectations related to city driving to guide users in expressing their input 
in a format compatible with the Input Formalization Language (FLI). 
Our approach has been successfully demonstrated through various non-trivial 
examples, showcasing its potential to address user input commonly encountered 
in city driving scenarios.

As large-scale quantum computing evolves, there is a critical need for efficient quantum error correction methods. Specifically, large-scale logical operations require considerable resources and introduce extensive gate cascades that are highly susceptible to errors. Therefore, a simplified approach known as quantum error reduction holds great potential. A recent variation of this approach, called the concealed inverses protocol, achieves significant reductions in gate counts, particularly when implementing the Fourier transform. In this work, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the protocol in a quantum device by using it to calculate the inverse of a specific matrix. Our results show that the gate-count efficiency of the protocol surpasses that of conventional quantum error correction methods, thereby facilitating the execution of complex operations on near-term quantum devices.

This paper investigates the ability to depict preorder relations using pseudoequivalences in regular categories. It begins by demonstrating that if a category E has pseudocartesian products, then the categories of preorders and categories with pseudoequivalences can be represented within E, respectively. Furthermore, the study reveals a relationship between preorder depictions in E and the presence of binary pseudoequivalences in E itself. Specifically, if all categories in a category E are regular and possess binary pseudoequivalences, then the depictions of preorders and equivalences within E are equivalent, a fact further supported by the observation that any two categories with the same objects in E are isomorphic, resulting in iso-completeness.

The application of multivariate spatial models to environmental issues, particularly in marine environments, has become increasingly prevalent due to the significant ecological and operational implications of extreme weather events. To effectively analyze and forecast the likelihood of catastrophic events in these environments, we have developed a flexible statistical framework that incorporates the Pearson III distribution and considers the interdependence of environmental variables across different geographical locations. By employing an advanced methodology that combines the Finite Mixture Explicit Representation and conditional peak over threshold estimation, we have been able to efficiently model extreme weather events without requiring computationally intensive simulations. Our approach is demonstrated through the examination of four datasets, including the well-known German North Sea, and two additional marine environments located in the UK and Australia, which highlight the practical viability and capabilities of the proposed method.

Recently, pre-trained CLIP models have significantly advanced computer vision performance in few-shot learning scenarios. However, models like CLIP, which use image and text embeddings, tend to struggle with generalizing to unfamiliar visual domains. To mitigate this issue, we introduce a novel approach that leverages visual influences on language to enhance these models. We utilize domain-specific images along with generated captions to create supplementary training pairs, thereby enabling visual extensions of pre-trained CLIP models without the need for labor-intensive annotations. This method focuses on dynamically identifying and incorporating new visual domains while also developing visual-centric language representations. The efficacy of our visual-enriched CLIP models is validated through impressive few-shot classification results on challenging datasets such as CUB, Stanford Birds, CARS, and ImageNet. Additionally, our approach yields substantial improvements on benchmark datasets within visual hamistics challenges, including the Stanford Cars and ImageNet LSUN benchmarks.

This study introduces an operator switching strategy for the Tracy-Singh matrix, a class of matrices with distinct diagonal blocks and zero off-diagonal blocks. Each block on the diagonal is a square matrix of the same size, while the remaining entries in the matrix are zeros. This matrix type is used in various practical applications, such as signal processing and quantum mechanics. By considering the noisy version of the Tracy-Singh matrix and its associated random operators, a new operator switching approach is developed for efficient simulation of the matrix and determination of limiting theorems. Numerical experiments validate the proposed method's performance.

We identify the topological segments of the quaternionic Eilenberg-Mac Lane spectra $X(\mathbb{H}/-)$, where the coefficients are given by the quaternian integers. The research in this study is based on the findings established in [KKL+15], and it involves the use of $\mathbb{RP}^1$-localization, a technique relying on the action of U(1) on complex Clifford complexes.

We establish a concept of compactness for local rings and show that several significant properties are implications of this compactness. The compactness of a local ring has the consequence that its prime spectrum carries the Zariski topology, a comprehensive description of its maximal ideal's fixed point set can be obtained from its Hilbert polynomial, its residue field is finitely generated, its weak uniform dimension equals one, its set of associated primes is finite, its set of edge primes is finite, its set of prime ideals is countable, its set of primary components is finite, its set of primary ideals corresponding to these components can be identified, a discrete valuation domain covering the ring is constructible, a complete pair covering the ring is constructible, and rings isolated from these valuations are constructibly discrete, respectively. The significance of compactness in ring theory lies in the fact that it enables us to reduce many difficult problems in the study of rings to the realm of Noetherian rings. The primary objective of this paper is to introduce the concept of compactness for local rings.

Machine learning techniques for medical image analysis are rapidly growing and numerous associated software tools are emerging. Currently, the exchange of learning results among researchers is primarily based on CSV files or visualizations, which restricts further analysis or comparison of results. To resolve this issue, a newly developed Python framework called Highdicom has been created to generate detailed learning results, including segmentation and classification outcomes, directly from neural network code, presenting them in an organized format via DICOM files. This implementation enables a wide range of outcomes to be easily accessed with standard DICOM tools, facilitating the development of detailed value sets and diagnostics tools for common errors in the reporting process.

We present detailed calculations for Noether charges associated with Einstein's general relativity, stemming from the Einstein-Hilbert action's surface term. We compare the different components of the surface term, deriving the Noether charge 2-form and its relation to the Schwarzschild entropy and a central charge in Viroro algebra. Our findings reveal that while a general surface term can be written in multiple equivalent forms, introducing a 2-form that equals zero on-shell renders the surface expression form-invariant and eliminates any surface contribution to conserved charges. We also derive the central charge in Viroro algebra in terms of entropy using a coordinate-independent method for Noether charge calculation, and note that this central charge is negative, in contrast to previous assumptions in Quantum Gravity. We find that the central charge is linearly dependent on entropy for Schwarzschild and de Sitter black holes, a result that is verified through direct calculations.

In recent years, deep learning models have gained significant attention in processing DNA sequences, but they require DNA sequence embedding models to generate high-quality vector representations. These embedding models, trained without labeled data, map DNA sequences to low-dimensional vectors based on their DNA sequence and structure, allowing for further analysis. By utilizing these vector representations, researchers can identify similar DNA sequences, detect patterns, and make DNA sequences amenable to further analysis and comparison.

The interaction between metal and oxide surfaces is highly dependent on the specific combination used, making it crucial to carefully choose the overlayer used to modify the surface for accurate measurements. Our study investigates the interaction between a (0001) Boule of V$_2$O$_3$ and various buffer layers and compares the results with the interaction between V$_2$O$_3$(0001) and metal layers. It is observed that various oxide modifications significantly shift the metal-insulator transition to lower temperatures compared to the interaction with metals, suggesting that the metal-insulator transition is highly sensitive to the specific conditions under which the phase transition occurs.

The Clebsch variable method, a widely recognized technique for reducing a system of equations of motion, is explored within the Lie-Poisson setting of geometric reduction. We demonstrate that introducing a specific type of connection variable, or 'clebsch-conjugation', inherently leads to symmetric reduction. This concept, inspired by a recent discovery in unconstrained mechanics, is illustrated by its application to Euler's equation on a Lie algebra. Furthermore, we demonstrate the effectiveness of this concept by deriving novel expressions for helicity in various fluid models.

Exoplanet research has significantly benefited from the extensive monitoring of over 800 fields by the Korean Microlensing Anomaly Net, observing the skies through all seasons at an impressive pace of 3.2 seconds per second. This effort has identified 2,018 suspected planets through irregularities in the data, of which we comprehensively analyzed a select 428 from outside the prime fields in our latest publication. The resulting discovery of 21 confirmed planets from this analysis further adds to our extensive catalogue of 1,017 planet candidates, including 58 confirmed ones, published previously. The latest findings highlight the importance of considering the intrinsic nature of the data and the observational limitations of the telescope's aperture, as well as the need to carefully choose fields with sufficient brightness levels for the project to be successful.

A new method for solving the compressible Navier-Stokes equations is explored, exploring how to maintain key physical principles, such as entropy and energy conservation, using an implicit time-stepping technique. We demonstrate that our algorithm effectively preserves these principles at the machine precision level even when using an implicitly time-discretized equation that does not inherently maintain conservation properties. Furthermore, our research shows that it's possible to implicitly time-discretize the pressure term without compromising entropy or energy conservation. We also present insights derived from both theoretical analysis and numerical experiments that may assist in developing implicit time-stepping methods for other thermodynamically governed systems.

The evaluation of algorithms for determining the chemical composition of unknown nuclear particles from their pulse shape characteristics is a crucial aspect of experiments, with machine learning techniques offering a promising approach. This study, conducted across multiple CNGS nuclear data sets, compared the effectiveness of four machine learning methods: Support Vector Machine, Random Forest, K-Nearest Neighbors, and Extreme Gradient Boosting, against traditional histogram analysis used in T2K experiment data. The research also investigated the importance of features and how this varies across the different machine learning methods employed.

A simultaneous expansion of symmetric functions in three distinct bases--those of elementary, homogeneous, and monomial symmetric functions--with parameters q and q^2 is explored. This expansion, known as the q,q^2-EEHm expansion, involves the q,q^2-eehm of semi-Dyck sequences. This concept builds on previous q,q^2-eehm expansions of symmetric functions, including those by Stembridge on 2-Dyck sequences and Berge on 1-Dyck sequences. This new expansion reveals that the q,q^2-eehm of a semi-Dyck sequence behaves similarly to the q,q^2-eehms in the q,q^2-Lavv numbers and q, q^2-Grassmann-Lavv numbers, marking the first known connection between q,q^2-eehms and q-rook polynomials. This connection is based on the notion that the q,q^2-eehms in semi-Dyck sequences correspond to a new class of board symmetries referred to as board-colored symmetries. This new theory of board-colored symmetries extends the existing q-ram theory and board-colored symmetries in Dyck sequences, discovered by Bevan and the second author, to a broader context.

Image recognition models, specifically convolutional neural networks (CNNs), are well-suited to extracting features from orientation-specific information in data. However, the parameter sharing, which is a fundamental aspect of CNNs, is limited by this same feature. To overcome this, the authors have developed a novel type of orientation-based architecture that utilizes orientation-specific components for its parameters, as well as biases and activations. The novel OConv architecture retains efficient, differentiable computation and, in experiments with data from the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets, the authors have observed considerable gains in performance when comparing models built with OConv to those built with standard CNNs, without any additional cost in terms of memory or computation.

A new type of curved linear interval is proposed in a suitable subset of homeomorphic transformations in the unit circle, leading to the definition of a novel relative trace equation. This equation utilizes a concept rooted in classical trace theory but tailored for this specific context. It is shown that all transformations satisfying the equation form a compact, convex set within the circle. This novel trace equation serves as a compactness-enforcing tool for constructing vanishing relative trace pairs, ultimately enabling the development of a novel Ruelle-type theorem for curved linear intervals. Additionally, this theorem is applied to transformations acting on the circle while excluding a Cantor set, with associated Ruelle-type estimates for associated Green functions.

We apply a substantial flavor dependence approach to model the cross-sections and kinematic distributions of the top quark, using four-momentum dependent parton distribution and fragmentation functions with no reference to specific partons. This allows us to draw general conclusions about the relationships between the masses of charged hadrons and their corresponding quarks. Using the masses of charged pions, kaons, and B-mesons, our calculation yields the mass of the top quark as 170.9 GeV, modified by the running coupling constant. Our analysis of the mass dependence on kinematic distributions reveals that the top quark's mass significantly impacts the Higgs boson's production rate, especially in the gluon-gluon fusion process. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the mass dependence also plays a role in the angular distributions of top quark pairs and other related observables. Our substantial flavor dependence approach offers a model-independent method to describe top quark physics.

We establish a condition under which a graph, almost regular in nature, can have its continuous values from the interval [0,1] assigned to edges such that every subset of its vertices has a associated value within this interval, related to differences of inverse square-root degrees of adjacent vertices in that subset. This result is further refined by demonstrating a specific instance where a uniform application of a constant value results in an edge-coloring without conflicts.

We establish a form of hypercontractivity for scaled Bergman spaces on the unit ball in $\mathbb{C}^d$, thereby extending the work of Gross in $L^p(\gamma_n)$ spaces and the findings of Boros, Prokof'ev, and Smirnov in two-dimensional Hardy spaces with scaled metrics.

A novel COVID-19 detection algorithm based on low-dose CT (LDCT) images is proposed, combining AI technology and medical expertise for pandemic management. To achieve this, a two-stage TDTCN model was developed. In the first stage, a feature extraction network was used to transform LDCT images into high-quality features, which were then scaled and vectorized. Subsequently, a contexture classification network was used for disease classification. To optimize the model, a novel loss function called TCN margin loss was introduced. Experimentally, our model demonstrated superior performance on multiple public COVID-19 datasets compared to other AI methods and medical template matching. These results validate the efficacy of our TDTCN approach in pandemic management.

The growing use of space-based services is being met with growing demand,
leading to the increasing deployment of on-orbit spacecraft. This paper
examines how this growing density of spacecraft impacts the available
orbital space, focusing particularly on the effects of varying spacecraft
sizes and the presence of spacecraft on their solar and gravitational orbits
in low-Earth orbit. We also discuss potential solutions, which could
potentially help resolve the current space debris issue.

Creating high-quality unstructured meshes on CAD models is a crucial yet challenging task. These meshes can be effectively used in various applications, such as simulations, but the process of generating high-order unstructured meshes on CAD models is currently hindered by several difficulties. One of the main challenges is that most mesh generators can only handle simplified CAD models, which often require the manual creation of a high-order unstructured mesh. In this paper, we propose a new method for creating high-order unstructured meshes on CAD models by first creating a coarse quadrilateral mesh that meets certain criteria and then refining it using finite element method. The method relies on a series of linear optimization problems, which can be solved efficiently and automatically. The proposed method has been tested on several 2D CAD models, such as those used in aerodynamics, and has been shown to produce high-quality unstructured meshes that are suitable for use in simulations.

The correlation coefficient plays a crucial role in various fields, especially in financial economics, where researchers focus on how assets behave in relation to one another. This has prompted researchers to explore how the correlation coefficient behaves in randomized versions of given datasets. Although earlier studies established the mean and variance for the correlation coefficient in specific dimensions, they did so only through theoretical reasoning, leaving out the mathematical formulas for calculating these values based on the dataset's size. This paper aims to fill this knowledge gap by deriving the mathematical formulas for the mean, variance, and skewness of the correlation coefficient in different dimensions, revealing the moments' dependence on the dataset's size. It also provides an alternative method using theoretical reasoning, validating the findings by comparing the calculated moments with simulated results. The paper's findings have practical implications in stochastic control theory and financial modeling, especially in understanding how to model and control the dynamics of multiple Brownian motions in a way that respects a given dataset's correlation structure.

The primary focus of this research is the application of the S-matrix approach to quantum field theory in the context of general relativity and string theory. Beginning with an overview, it delves into scattering amplitude techniques in quantum field theory and how they can be applied to compute the effective action of Einstein's gravity. Subsequently, a detailed introduction to string amplitudes is provided, highlighting their connection to scattering amplitudes in quantum field theory. Consequently, it enables a calculation of the stringy corrections to the Einstein's action.

We introduce a novel finite-dimensional interior localized feedback control scheme for the Navier-Stokes equations in three dimensions. This control mechanism has been shown to apply across various fluid properties $p\in[2,\infty]$. Specifically, we demonstrate the existence of a uniform stabilization system within critical Sobolev and Besov space frameworks. This new result is the first of its kind for the $p=\infty$ case with an interior control, and is built on the existence of a universal attractor within these spaces for the controlled Navier-Stokes system. We establish the existence of a uniform stabilization system using a target tracking approach and show the existence of a target system whose long-term dynamics reside within a compact, invariant, invariant set within a modified Banach space that includes the critical Sobolev and Besov spaces as subspaces.

Literature is widely regarded as a mirror to society, and digital archives of literary works are now commonplace, however creating a dictionary from such works remains a complicated process due to variations in spelling and vocabulary throughout history. Researchers have traditionally relied on established literary collections such as the Early English Text Society and The Oxford English Dictionary for accurate representations of historical word usage patterns, but these resources are difficult to replicate without direct access. This study utilizes a large collection of publicly available works from LitMind to generate a dictionary, leveraging computational methods to extract word forms and frequency data. A web-based dictionary is created and made accessible to users, showcasing the capabilities of open literary archives and advancing our understanding of historical language usage through data-driven research.

A key aspect of recommending systems is their capacity to adapt to individual users' preferences and explainable AI aims to clarify how recommendations are tailored to specific users. However, there is a lack of a standardized approach for modeling the relationships between users in explainable recommendation systems. We introduce a new framework for the LIME recommendation interpretation, focusing on its ability to provide meaningful insights into how the models account for user preferences and the effects of different user characteristics on these preferences, using a case study on a movie recommendation system to illustrate our points.

Quantum wells near the band edge of a semiconductor have been widely used in various applications. Near the interface, however, there is a problem with the quantum well's electron level being raised higher due to the difference in midgap states' fermi levels between the two materials. To address this issue, a new theoretical model has been proposed for near surface InAs quantum wells within an GaInAs substrate. This model takes into account the energy levels of the midgap states in near surface InAs and how they interact with the quantum well's electron level, allowing it to be more accurately represented. By adjusting the electron level's height based on the midgap states' influence, a stable electron level can be achieved at the desired height.

In the context of non-iid data, our research investigates the interplay between regional query sampling and federated learning, where data is divided into regions with queries drawn from different regions, allowing us to analyze the process. We have developed a mathematical model where each region's parameters are tracked and the update process is simulated, where regional sample sizes and regions differ. We have derived two critical findings, where two key theorts stipulate the conditions under which regional sample sizes and regions significantly impact the learning process, where these findings shed light on the performance of regional queries in federated learning and suggest a more general approach for handling non-iid data.

The recent development of "Rapid Sinkhorn" by Exakdov et al. exposed an overlooked property in the analysis of optimal transport algorithms, specifically "Sinkhorn-Knott-Rose" and "KS-IR". A key discovery in "Rapid Sinkhorn" involved showing that a certain pattern in the Hessian of the Sinkhorn map leads to an eigenvalue of 2 at 2 for large optimal transport plans, resulting in the Hessian having a null direction and causing slow convergence in the KS-IR algorithm. Building upon this discovery, we identified a new class of plans, specifically "collinear triangular arrays", that also possess a null direction in the Hessian and thus experience the same slow convergence rate. The key insight into these plans lies in their linear growth pattern along one axis, influenced by a specific pattern, $\Lambda$, and their growth rate, $\rho(\Lambda)$, which determines the growth rate of their singular values and leads to the appearance of a new class of eigenvalues in the Hessian. The article presents an algorithm to construct these plans and discusses potential applications in machine learning and computer vision.

The young star AU Mic is notable for its frequent and powerful flares, 
which significantly impact surrounding planets AU Mic b and c. These flares can 
alter the physical properties of planetary rings and disintourage the growth of 
planetesimals, while also affecting the potential habitability of AU Mic c. 
Despite these flares being prominent in the optical spectrum, their frequency and 
intensity are not well understood in the far ultraviolet (FUV) spectrum. This 
study presents the discovery of FUV flares from AU Mic, detected by the Far 
Ultraviolet Spectroscopic Telescope (FUSTE), which occurred with similar 
recurrence and duration as the optical flares. Observations of a quiescent phase 
of AU Mic revealed that the FUV emission is dominated by the activity of the 
star's chromosphere, with the level of coronal activity being minimal. Based 
on this finding, a model of AU Mic's chromospheric activity is used to predict 
the expected FUV emission from quiescent states and future flares.

The concept of radiation response drag, first introduced in 2004, has been further developed with a focus on the electron-ion plasma. A detailed analysis of the consequences for an electromagnetic plane wave in a cold plasma has been performed, demonstrating that under specific conditions, the plasma behaves as if it were a piece of metal with the properties of electrical resistance. As a plane wave propagates through such a plasma, the process becomes irreversible due to the plasma's electrons experiencing an asymmetric force opposing the wave, resulting in the generation of entropy and dissipation of the wave, ultimately leading to the asymptotic cessation of the wave as energy transferred to the plasma is gradually absorbed by the particles.

In the realm of data analysis and machine learning, missing values significantly impact outcomes due to their critical role in the underlying statistical models. This research aims to develop a new approach for handling datasets with unequal distribution, specifically missing data. Nearest neighbor classification methods are widely used in machine learning due to their simplicity and effectiveness. However, these methods typically assume evenly distributed data and, as a result, exhibit poor performance when presented with incomplete datasets. To address this limitation, a novel approach is introduced to handle unequal distribution during the preprocessing phase before applying the nearest neighbor classification algorithm. Experimental findings from real-world and simulated data sets indicate that the proposed approach outperforms existing methods. Furthermore, a simulation study is conducted to demonstrate the superior predictive accuracy of the proposed approach, revealing that it achieves approximately a 10% increase in prediction accuracy.

We introduce a new set of 18 high-redshift quasars ($z > 2.5$) with exceptional brightness ($i'_{AB} < 18.5$), discovered by the SkyMapper survey, as well as 11 additional quasars ($z > 2.5$) with brightness exceeding 19. These new quasars, along with 14 previously identified in the ZQSO2 sample, were further analyzed and cross-checked through spectroscopic verification. The resulting dataset of 43 quasars ($1.5 < z < 3.5$) encompasses the most comprehensive collection of quasars identified to date through optical spectroscopy, surpassing the capabilities of SDSS and Pantheon. The comprehensive zQSO2 sample, incorporating 24 new members, now spans the entire known quasars' luminosity distribution ($\log(L/D_{L, \odot}) < 11.5$), allowing us to study the properties of dim quasars in greater depth. The study reveals that dim quasars are predominantly composed of low-luminosity Seyfert galaxies, characterized by a mean redshift of 2.3, whereas the most luminous quasars shine brightly ($\log(L/D_{L, \odot}) > 12.5$) and are located at higher redshifts ($z > 2.5$). The study also explores the physical characteristics of these luminous

We have developed a theoretical model to analyze the behavior of a specific type of nanoscale device consisting of a quantum dot connected to a superconducting island via a tunnel junction. This setup differs from traditional Josephson junctions, as it involves a smaller quantum dot instead of a superconducting junction base. Our model predicts the charge tunneling spectrum of the system, which can be affected by the superconducting gap in the island, and this spectrum can be detected using another tunnel junction within the device as a readout mechanism. This setup provides an alternative method to investigate charge tunneling phenomena that may be inaccessible through other methods, such as Coulomb blockade or the Kondo effect.

We examine the contraction properties of preservative differential equation solutions as the parameter approaches infinity. This involves studying systems of preservation laws in one space dimension and introducing new contraction metrics tailored to intrinsic preservative variables. By establishing contracted characteristics for preservative solutions, we aim to illuminate the unique entropy discontinuities associated with preservation equations. Specifically, we on offer a stored mass functional that provides the entropy discontinuity criterion, analogous to the Entropy solution in classical conservation laws.

Creating a complete 360-degree view from a single image is a challenging but beneficial process for numerous applications, particularly in virtual reality. Currently, this process is typically carried out by combining images taken from different perspectives. However, this paper presents an innovative method that utilizes only a single image as input, leveraging advanced AI models to generate a complete 360-degree view efficiently and accurately. Our approach achieves this by developing a novel neural network that employs advanced AI techniques to map features from a single image to a 360-degree view, significantly reducing computational costs and enhancing performance on real-world datasets.

This paper presents an evidence-based approach to predicting, improving and managing the behavior of complex systems composed of interconnected processes. To demonstrate the feasibility of achieving these goals using solely data-driven methods, we have developed a networked SIS epidemic model comprising simple units connected through a predetermined or uncertain network. These units are given initial conditions based on historical data, allowing us to test the proposed forecasting framework without relying on knowledge of the system's internal dynamics. Initially, we evaluate our framework's ability to provide accurate system-level predictions. Subsequently, we investigate the optimal control strategies required to identify the most critical units for public health and to develop interventions that minimize disease transmission. These controls involve implementing targeted protection measures, such as social distancing, to address both known and unknown connectivity. The results indicate that our framework can provide accurate predictions, identify critical units, and develop effective regulations using solely data-driven methods.

We've studied experimentally and numerically the behavior of a droplet on a fiber.
The investigation involved analyzing the dynamics of a liquid layer on a fiber.
In contrast to the traditional understanding of droplet formation on fibers, our research revealed that slip at the fiber's surface significantly affects the process.
The presence of slip significantly shortens the time it takes for the instability to occur, which challenges the widely accepted understanding of droplet formation on fibers.
The effect of slip was observed to be more pronounced under certain conditions.
Specifically, the onset of the instability was found to be delayed when the fiber's surface had minimal slip.
However, the observed phenomenon differed significantly from the previously established results, which showed that droplet formation occurs at a longer wavelength in the absence of slip.
The current study involved both numerical simulations and experimental observations of the liquid layer on a fiber.
The simulations were conducted using a commercial software, which allowed for a detailed analysis of the liquid's behavior.
The experimental setup involved a fiber submerged in a liquid, which was then analyzed using high-speed imaging.
The results showed that droplet formation occurs at a much shorter wavelength than previously thought, which was found to be a direct consequence of slip at the fiber's surface.

This study establishes that the flow of vector fields, defined by coefficients that are Lipschitz functions, preserves the Lipschitz norm of distributional solutions to the Hunter-Saxton equation, even when slight variations in the equation's coefficients occur. This outcome enhances previous findings by Hunter and Saxton, particularly their use of a specific norm for rotationally invariant distributions. Furthermore, our results demonstrate a continuous dependence of the equation's flow on its input data, measured in Lipschitz metrics.

Assessing scoliosis through ultrasonography can be an efficient alternative to radiography, which carries certain risks and often proves more accessible. Although the manual process of scanning is often labor-intensive and relies on the expertise of the sonographer, the design of ultrasonography systems has historically prioritized image quality, neglecting reliability in the process. This study aims to develop a novel ultrasonography system, specifically designed to minimize user error and enhance the consistency of the measurement, thereby reducing the QoF ratio - a key indicator of scanning reliability - to around 0.15. By employing a combination of mechanical features to guide the transducer and intelligent software to optimize its positioning and provide real-time feedback, this system successfully achieves a QoF ratio of approximately 0.16.

This research introduces an innovative approach for determining synthetic speech duration using a non-statistical model. Traditional duration prediction methods typically rely on statistical models, which can be resource-intensive and difficult to optimize. In contrast, the proposed approach employs a median-driven strategy to efficiently determine optimal acoustic model parameters. By utilizing the mean speaker-specific speech durations, this method can accurately replicate the desired syllable and word lengths in the synthetic speech, thus eliminating the need for a separate mean value for each phoneme. Additionally, the efficacy of the introduced median-driven strategy is evaluated through listening tests and the results demonstrate its practical feasibility and performance advantages.

The digital world has become a breeding ground for harmful online speech, particularly hate speech, which is particularly prevalent on social media platforms. This speech poses a serious threat to users and is also considered illegal, making its detection and prevention a top priority. Detecting hate speech on the web is particularly challenging due to its ever-changing nature and subtlety, which often goes unnoticed. To address this issue, researchers have developed a novel system called Characteristic Extraction (CharEx) for identifying and categorizing online hate speech. CharEx uses a novel feature called character-level word (CW) embeddings, a form of word representation that captures nuanced details and rare words that other methods fail to capture. CW embeddings are trained using fastText, a framework that excels at identifying rare words and contextual information, and are then used to train word and character-based Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks. This framework enables the identification of new hate categories and provides flexibility in model design. CharEx outperformed state-of-the-art systems on standard datasets such as ABUSENB and Twitterhate, demonstrating the potential of using CW embeddings and novel feature combinations in NLP.

This research paper explores the potential of exchanging characteristic information in MIMO systems. The central challenge lies in optimizing the selection and order of transmitted reference symbol sequences to minimize interantenna cross talk. This problem is formulated as a discrete optimization issue. A novel and efficient algorithm is proposed to resolve this problem, which also sheds light on practical design considerations for MIMO systems utilizing transmitting antennas with unique characteristics.

There are numerous digital archives featuring medieval and Renaissance handwritten manuscripts, but their locations and accessibility are often unclear, with many still residing in physical form. The explosion of digital archives has spurred numerous researchers to tackle complex tasks like pattern recognition, text extraction, and understanding of handwritten manuscripts. This work provides a comprehensive overview of the digital archives medieval and Renaissance written languages, aiming to assist researchers in accessing tasks and participants with varying levels of annotation.

Robot joint performance is hindered by friction, causing inconsistencies and control issues that can be represented by the Spreeuw-de Man-Heuvel-Sanderson (SMS) model. Although this model helps to better understand friction, it's too complex for practical control systems, especially with the many friction parameters involved. In this paper, we introduce a novel approach to friction compensation, focusing on the performance of industrial robots. We use the concept of flatness to create parameterized trajectories that can minimize acceleration, simplifying the control process. These trajectories, despite being open-loop, outperform the traditional PID control system, especially during rapid movements. Additionally, we incorporate sensor data to continuously adjust the system and provide real-time feedback. Our results, supported by simulations and experimental data, show the effectiveness of this approach in improving robot performance.

Evaluating the intricate relationships between various states of health and survival, especially in patients who have experienced a myocardial infarction, presents a significant challenge.  A new method for analyzing complex patient data has been developed to study these relationships.  This method uses joint modeling, which models the dynamic nature of health conditions and the time until key events occur, such as a hospital readmission.  A specific application demonstrates how this approach can be used to study the effect of living settings on the likelihood of readmission in patients who have experienced a myocardial infarction.  A large database of patients who have experienced a myocardial residential relocation is used to create a dynamic feature that considers how long the patient has been living in their home.  This approach allows researchers to identify critical periods of adaptation after relocation and to identify the most effective policies to improve patient outcomes.  A significant advantage is that this method can be applied to a wide range of populations experiencing multiple life events.

The concept of molecular continua, where liquids are modeled as homogeneous media with a molecular radius $r_m$, has received increased attention in recent years. This approach, where the inner boundary of the outer continuum is determined by the van der Waals radii of the solute atoms, is utilized to establish boundary conditions for the Poisson-Boltzmann equation in biomolecular simulations, utilizing the PyPBOLB library. However, an open-source Python module, based on the PYPBOLB source code, specifically addresses the calculation of the multi-site van-der-Waals outer boundary potential and its gradient for multiple solute atoms, utilizing the Delaunay triangulation algorithm. This module, named 'py-mcow', fills a critical gap in the PyPBOLB source code, which previously lacked support for multi-site outer boundary calculations. This module, with its corresponding test suite, is available under the BSD-2-Clause license and can be integrated into external, independent electrostatics libraries for the calculation of multi-site molecular outer boundary potentials and their gradients.

We explore the solution to a long-established problem in graph theory, specifically the well-known graph labeling problem, with a focus on creating a mapping that uniquely identifies a graph through its distances to selected nodes. A research hypothesis, the Rado conjecture, has driven previous studies, proposing an algorithmic solution where, in general, the problem proves intractable but potentially manageable in graphs characterized by specific structural attributes. A parameterized complexity version of the Rado conjecture was formulated by Rosamond et al., suggesting an algorithmic solution where the complexity is determined by the size of a 'feedback vertex group' - a specific set of vertices whose removal results in disconnected components for which the labeling requirement is no longer applicable. A different approach to this concept, the 'modulated feedback vertex group', was introduced, offering an even finer structural description. Building on previous work, we prove that this new 'modulated feedback vertex group' can effectively replace the previously proposed concept in the Rado conjecture parameterization, thus providing a solution. This new result has a significant implication where, in graphs characterized by a small 'modulated feedback vertex group', an efficient solution to the labeling problem is achievable through the creation of a bounded search tree, enabling polynomial time when considering the summation of specific attributes.
